lead: A body loaded at only two points has a simple rule: the two forces must lie on the line joining the points. A body loaded with three coplanar forces in equilibrium has a related rule: the three lines of action meet at one point, or all run parallel. These rules give the direction of an unknown hinge reaction before you solve equations, and they expose a wrong free body diagram fast. They are used in links, brackets, tie rods and machine frames.

blocks.text: A two-force body is a rigid body acted on by forces at only two points. It has no applied couple, and its own weight is neglected or already counted in the two forces. Let the points be A and B. The line of action is the infinite line along which a force acts.

Take moments about A. The force at A has zero moment about A. For total moment to be zero, the force at B must also have zero moment about A. For a non-zero force, that is possible only if its line of action passes through A. By the same argument about B, the force at A acts along AB. So both forces act along the line joining the two points.
Force equilibrium then makes them equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The member is in tension if the forces pull A and B apart, and in compression if they push them together.

Common two-force members: a short link in a frame, a tie rod, a cable with no distributed load, and a bar loaded only at its two pin joints. A beam carrying its own weight is not a two-force body. Neither is a shaft with a torque, nor a bar with a load at a third point.

blocks.where: F<sub>A</sub> is the force at A, F<sub>B</sub> is the force at B, and the minus sign means opposite direction.

blocks.text: A three-force body has three coplanar forces acting on it and no applied couple. If it is in equilibrium, the three lines of action are concurrent (meet at one point) or parallel.

Proof for the concurrent case: let the lines of F<sub>1</sub> and F<sub>2</sub> meet at O. Take moments about O. F<sub>1</sub> and F<sub>2</sub> pass through O, so their moments about O are zero. The total moment must be zero, so F<sub>3</sub> must also have zero moment about O. A non-zero force has zero moment about O only when its line of action passes through O. Hence all three lines meet at O.

If F<sub>1</sub> and F<sub>2</sub> are parallel, they meet at infinity. Then F<sub>3</sub> must also be parallel to them. Three parallel forces can balance: two upward at the ends and one downward between them, with magnitudes fixed by force and moment equations.

Use the rule to find the direction of a hinge reaction. In a bracket hinged at A, pulled by a cable at B and loaded by weight at G, extend the cable line and the weight line to P. The hinge reaction at A must act along AP. You still find its magnitude from equilibrium equations. Some syllabi call this a three-force member; others just say three coplanar forces in equilibrium.

items: Draw the free body diagram and mark every line of action.
Count the forces. Two points only and no couple means a two-force member.
For three coplanar forces, extend two known lines to their intersection P.
Draw the unknown reaction through P, or parallel to the other two if they are parallel.
Take moments about a point that removes one unknown, then use force equilibrium.

blocks.text: The rules give directions, not magnitudes. A common error is to stop after drawing the reaction line. You must still satisfy ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0 and ΣM = 0.

In the rod example below, the weight line is vertical at x = 0.5 m and the string line is horizontal at y = 1.732 m. Their intersection is P = (0.5, 1.732) m. The hinge reaction line is AP. That one geometric fact turns a three-unknown problem into a simple moment equation.

figure.caption: The three lines of action meet at O, the point used in the moment proof. If any line missed O, that force would have a non-zero moment about O and equilibrium would fail.

spec.aria: Three forces acting at points A, B and C all have lines of action that pass through the single point O.

examples.question: A uniform rod AB of length 2 m and weight 300 N is hinged to a vertical wall at A. End B is above A and held by a horizontal string. The rod makes 30° with the wall. Find the string tension and the hinge reaction.
steps: Take A as origin, x to the right, y upward. B is at (2 sin30, 2 cos30) = (1.0, 1.732) m.
Weight W = 300 N acts vertically through the midpoint, whose x-coordinate is 1 sin30 = 0.5 m. Its line of action is x = 0.5 m.
The string at B is horizontal, so its line of action is y = 1.732 m.
The weight line and string line meet at P = (0.5, 1.732) m. By the three-force rule, the hinge reaction at A acts along AP. Its angle θ from the wall is tanθ = 0.5/1.732 = 0.2887, so θ = 16.1°.
Take moments about A. The perpendicular distance from A to the string line is 1.732 m; from A to the weight line is 0.5 m. The string tension T acts left. T(1.732) = 300(0.5).
Force equilibrium: R<sub>x</sub> = T = 86.6 N to the right, R<sub>y</sub> = W = 300 N upward.
R = √(86.6² + 300²) = 312.2 N. Its direction is the same 16.1° from the wall.
examples.answer: The string tension is 86.6 N, and the hinge reaction is 312.2 N acting at 16.1° from the wall.
examples.check:
import math
L = 2.0
W = 300.0
ang = math.radians(30.0)
xB = L * math.sin(ang)
yB = L * math.cos(ang)
xW = (L / 2.0) * math.sin(ang)
T = W * xW / yB
Rx = T
Ry = W
R = math.hypot(Rx, Ry)
theta = math.degrees(math.atan2(Rx, Ry))
print(f'{T:.1f}')
print(f'{R:.1f}')
print(f'{theta:.1f}')

traps: Calling a member two-force when it carries weight, a couple, or a load at a third point.
Treating two-force forces as merely concurrent. They must be collinear along the line joining the loaded points.
Using three-force concurrency when the forces are not coplanar or when an applied couple acts.
In the rod example, taking the moment arm of the string as 2 m. The perpendicular distance is 2 cos30 = 1.732 m.
Drawing the hinge reaction along the rod. In a three-force problem its line is set by the intersection of the other two lines, not by the member axis.

quiz.q: Define a two-force body and state the direction of its two forces.
quiz.a: Forces at only two points, no couple, weight neglected; the two forces are equal, opposite and act along the line joining the points.

quiz.q: Why must the two forces in a two-force body be collinear?
quiz.a: Taking moments about one loaded point, the other force must have zero moment about it; so its line of action must pass through that point.

quiz.q: A two-force link has a 5 kN force at each end. What is the force in the link and along what line?
quiz.a: 5 kN along the line joining the two points; tension or compression depending on the sense of the end forces.

quiz.q: A bar has forces at three points and also carries a pure couple. Can you use the three-force concurrency rule? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The couple adds a moment that does not vanish at the intersection point, so the third force line need not pass through it.

quiz.q: Can three coplanar forces in equilibrium be all parallel? Give the arrangement.
quiz.a: Yes. Two upward at the ends and one downward between them, with magnitudes set by ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0.

quiz.q: In a three-force body, two known lines of action meet at P. What is the line of action of the third force?
A member has forces at only two points but also carries its own weight. Is it a two-force body? Why?
quiz.a: No. The weight is a third force, distributed along the member, so the two end forces need not be collinear and equal.

beyond: Not for the exam. In structural software, the two-force rule helps identify axial members before a full stiffness analysis. The three-force rule is the geometric basis of graphic statics and funicular polygons, used to design masonry arches and cable nets. Search 'graphic statics', 'funicular polygon' and 'three-force member concurrency' to go further. In robotics, the concurrency test is applied to each rigid link when checking static equilibrium under three applied forces.
